checkpoints: Contract signature: `AccessibleSortableList<T>({ items, getId, onReorder, renderItem, activation?, announcements? })`.

The component owns the whole dnd-kit tree — `DndContext` with `closestCenter`, `SortableContext` with the vertical strategy, and one `onDragEnd` that maps `active`/`over` through `arrayMove` and calls `onReorder(newItems)` exactly once — so consumers never see raw drag events.

Both sensors are hardwired: `PointerSensor` with a tunable activation constraint (distance ~5px default, a delay option for touch) and `KeyboardSensor` with `sortableKeyboardCoordinates`; keyboard support is not a prop, because "forgot the `KeyboardSensor`" is precisely the failure this component exists to prevent.
Each row is wrapped by an internal sortable shell that keeps the activator flat — `setNodeRef` + `attributes` + `listeners` on one focusable element, with `transform`/`transition` wired to `style`.
`renderItem` only fills the visual interior of the row, so the consumer's markup can never detach the Space key (or any activator) from the sensor the way the hand-rolled version did.
The `announcements` prop customizes what the live region speaks per phase (meaningful item names), but the region itself can't be disabled through the API.
Defense of the design: dragEnd-only commit buys Escape-cancel and focus stability for free, and the rigidity of baked-in sensors is the point.

States the signature `useFocusTrap({ active, onEscape, enabled? })` returning a `RefObject` — a markup-agnostic container ref the consumer attaches itself (works the same for a modal, drawer, or command palette).
On activation, the hook saves `document.activeElement` as the trigger element, then moves focus to the first focusable element inside the container.
While open, the focusable-element list is recomputed live on every Tab keydown (via `querySelectorAll`) instead of being cached once, because dialog content can change between keystrokes.

Boundary wrapping is explicit: Tab on the last focusable element jumps to the first, Shift+Tab on the first jumps to the last, plus a `!container.contains(activeElement)` check that pulls focus back in if it escapes.
On close, the hook restores focus to the saved trigger element, and defines a fallback (e.g. a stable landmark) for when that trigger has since been removed from the DOM.
Esc only calls `onEscape()` — the hook never closes anything itself, so the actual close/state-ownership stays with each parent component.
The hook sets no ARIA attributes at all (no `role`, `aria-modal`, `aria-labelledby`) — those stay on each consumer's own markup since they differ per surface.

`onEscape`/`enabled` are read through refs updated every render while the effect's dependency array stays `[active]` only, so a new inline `onEscape` from the parent doesn't tear down and re-arm the trap mid-open.
This is the WAI-ARIA combobox-controlling-listbox pattern, not an ordinary mouse menu.

The input carries `role=combobox` and always keeps DOM focus; the "active" option is merely a virtual cursor, so Arrow keys only change `aria-activedescendant` on the input plus `aria-selected` on the option, letting the user type to filter and arrow through results at the same time without the two fighting.

The screen reader announces the newly active option because the changed attribute (`aria-activedescendant`) lives on the element that is actually focused — the input, not the option — which is why typing and arrowing don't fight each other for the screen reader either.

cmdk's primitives (`Command.Input`/`List`/`Group`/`Item`) attach all of those roles automatically; the remaining work is supplying a stable value per item so the fuzzy filter ranks correctly, plus an `onSelect` for the action that runs when the item is chosen.

The shortcut is a single document-level keydown listener checking `metaKey || ctrlKey`, calling `preventDefault` because the browser also claims Ctrl+K by default, mounted exactly once so it works on every route with no duplicate listeners.
The dialog chrome traps focus while open and, on ESC, restores focus to the exact element that triggered the palette — the standard focus lifecycle of an accessible dialog.
Enter runs the active item's `onSelect` and then closes the palette.
Frames `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` as an accessibility contract to honor (not a nice-to-have), tied to the concrete risk that a large shared-layoutId morph can trigger vestibular symptoms.

Detects the preference by reading `window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches` synchronously inside the `useState` initializer — not only inside a `useEffect` — so the correct value is already set on the very first render, before any morph frame can render.
Also subscribes to the media query's `change` event so a live OS-level toggle mid-session takes effect immediately, without requiring a remount.

When reduced, drops the shared `layoutId` from both the card and the modal so framer-motion has no shared element to FLIP between — the modal simply appears/disappears rather than morphing out of the card.
The reduced path also forces the modal's enter/exit to an instant, opacity-only transition (e.g. `duration: 0`) — explicitly not just a shortened version of the same morph animation.
Exposes the reduced/full decision as an inspectable flag (e.g. a `data-reduced` attribute) so the state can be checked by tooling/tests instead of judged from pixels.

Verifies with an automated test that emulates reduced motion (e.g. Playwright `page.emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: "reduce" })`) and samples the element's bounding box over time to confirm zero animation delta, rather than relying on a single static screenshot.
Position: against the teammate's argument that arrayMove should run on every dragMove event.
Visual mechanism: the mid-drag move is a CSS transform from useSortable (CSS.Transform.toString) — GPU-composited and cheap.
Structural invariant: DOM order and React keys stay unchanged during the drag — only the CSS transform moves.
Commit point: arrayMove runs exactly once, in onDragEnd — one input-agnostic commit point shared by pointer and keyboard, not on every dragMove.
Breakage — Focus: the dragged card is the focused activator, so reordering the DOM mid-drag rips focus away from the keyboard user mid-gesture.

Breakage — Cancel: Escape restores the original order for free only because state was never touched (Flow 3's chip still reads a,b,c after cancel); per-move commits would force a manual reverse-mutation.
Premise rebuttal: "DOM must match visuals" is wrong — the transform IS the visual, deliberately decoupled from structure until the user confirms by dropping.
Honest cost: transform/transition must still be applied to style manually, or cards teleport instead of gliding.

Bottom line: both reports are consistent with a focus trap working 100% correctly, because the trap governs exactly one channel — the physical Tab key, via keydown, intercepting at the two dialog boundaries — and knows nothing about the mouse or how screen readers browse.

Screen-reader hole: assistive tech has a browse mode — a reading cursor moving through the accessibility tree without needing Tab — so that user simply read straight past the dialog into the content behind it.
Screen-reader fix: role="dialog" together with aria-modal="true" tells AT that everything outside the dialog is inert and must not be read.
Naming requirement: a complete dialog also needs an accessible name via aria-labelledby, since aria-modal alone doesn't tell AT what the dialog is.

Mouse hole: aria-modal is only a promise made to assistive tech and blocks no pointer event, so the background still needs a genuine full-cover overlay or the inert attribute for a click to actually be disabled.

Synthesis: a complete modal is three separate mechanisms — Tab interception for the keyboard, aria-modal for assistive tech, and overlay/inert for the mouse — omitting any one lets that specific layer leak even while the others work perfectly.
Verification: a keyboard-only walk confirms the trap, VoiceOver/NVDA turned on catches read-past, and an axe-core scan checks the ARIA structure — none of the three checks proves the other two.

Cost of direct animation: layout properties like width/top sit at the top of the rendering pipeline's cost — changing them forces re-layout, then repaint, then composite, per frame, so a 60fps morph is 60 reflows a second that janks a mid-range phone.
FLIP technique: measure the box before (First) and after (Last) the change, apply an Inverse translate+scale so nothing visibly moved, then Play that transform to zero.
Why FLIP is cheap: only transform and opacity ever animate, and those composite on the GPU without touching layout.
Shared layoutId mechanism: matching ids across two elements make framer-motion treat the card and the modal as one element that moved, morphing between their boxes.
Shared layoutId constraint: only one visible element per layoutId is allowed at a time.
Exit-animation gap: CSS transitions can't animate exit at all since React unmounts instantly, which is why AnimatePresence exists to defer that unmount.

Senior caveat: FLIP isn't free — it reads geometry and writes transforms per element, so hundreds of simultaneously-animating layout elements burn main-thread time, meaning the layout prop should be scoped to the elements that matter.
Verification: proof lives in the Performance panel as composite work with zero per-frame Layout events.

Narrowing via pointer working: pointer drag success exonerates the context, both sensor registrations, and onDragEnd, placing the break between the keyboard user's focus and dnd-kit's keyboard handler, inside the item itself.
Root cause in code: setNodeRef is on the outer <li>, but attributes and listeners are spread onto an inner <div> behind the Card chrome instead.

Why this breaks keyboard: dnd-kit binds keyboard activation to the node it ref'd, and since the element that actually receives focus and the Space keypress is not that node, KeyboardSensor never hears the activation.
Why pointer still works: pointer events bubble regardless of where they started, which is why the mouse still works fine despite the mismatch.
Fix: make ONE flat element the activator — setNodeRef, {...attributes}, and {...listeners} all on the same <li>, with no focus-owning wrapper in between.
Verification flow: focus the card, press Space to get aria-pressed="true" plus a "picked up" announcement, ArrowDown, then Space to drop and see the order chip flip.
Regression guard: lock the flow in as a Playwright spec, because this class of failure is invisible to eyeball QA.
Diagnosis pattern: the only-first-open, only-reduce-users symptom indicates the gate is wrong for exactly one render.
Root cause: the hook seeds useState(false) and reads matchMedia only inside useEffect, so React commits the first render with reduced=false.
Consequence of that first render: with reduced=false, layoutId is present and framer-motion begins the FLIP morph on that very first render.
Why later opens are fine: useEffect flips the flag to true only after paint, which is why every subsequent open is instant.
Fix: make the read synchronous via useState(() => window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches), guarded for typeof window, keeping the change listener for live OS toggles.
Effect of the fix: the very first render now drops layoutId and renders the opacity-only, zero-duration path from the start.

Verification: under emulateMedia({ reducedMotion: "reduce" }), the first click shows data-reduced="true" immediately and repeated bounding-box samples don't drift, plus toggling the OS setting live confirms the subscription still fires.
Stakes: this matters because the flash lands on vestibular-sensitive users, the one audience that must never see it.

The focus trap caches its focusable-elements list once in the effect when the dialog opens, but the dialog's content is live (a button can go from enabled to disabled, an input can mount) — so the stored first/last elements go stale, breaking the boundary-wrapping logic and causing Tab to get stuck on a now-disabled element or leak past the real last element; fix by recomputing the focusable list inside the Tab keydown handler itself every time, never caching it across the dialog's open lifetime.

role="dialog" with no aria-labelledby or aria-label means a screen reader announces an empty, unnamed dialog — an axe-core violation; fix by pointing aria-labelledby at the id of the heading inside the dialog.

The missing aria-modal="true" means a screen reader's browse mode reads straight past the dialog into the background page, since the Tab trap alone only constrains the physical Tab key and says nothing to assistive tech about the rest of the page being inert; fix by adding aria-modal="true".

The focus lifecycle is entirely absent: nothing saves document.activeElement when the dialog opens, and onClose just sets open to false with no .focus() call anywhere, so every close drops focus to <body> and the next Tab a keyboard user presses restarts from the very top of the page, losing their place completely; fix by saving the trigger element on open, calling .focus() on it in the cleanup/close path, and falling back to a stable landmark like <main> if that saved element is no longer in the DOM by the time the dialog closes.

Ranking: all three findings are user-breaking, not nitpicks — the stale cache and the missing focus restore are worst because they actively strand a keyboard user, while the missing name/modal is a close second because it breaks the experience specifically for screen-reader users.

Before approving, the reviewer wants evidence, not just the diff: a live keyboard-only walkthrough (Tab cycling inside the dialog, Shift+Tab wrapping at the first element back to the last, Esc or Close restoring focus to the exact trigger) plus an axe-core scan reporting zero violations.
